Factors that upregulate Naþ reabsorption are cytosolic acidosis, Angiotensin II and sympathetic innervation. Factors that down-
regulate it are cytosolic alkalosis, dopamine and PTH (parathyroid hormone). Water moves along with sodium, so that in the
permeable proximal tubule, H2O gets proportionally reabsorbed and the osmolality at the end of the proximal tubule remains
isotonic.
Loop of Henle
The loop of Henle contributes 20–30% of sodium reabsorption. The thin descending limb is water permeable due to the presence of
aquaporin-1, but impermeable to solutes. The ascending limb on the contrary is impermeable to water and the main site of Naþ
reabsorption, especially in the thick ascending limb (TAL). In this segment, sodium reabsorption is driven again by the Na⁺/K⁺-
ATPase. On the luminal membrane, Naþ absorption occurs via the Naþ/Kþ/2Cl Co-Transporter (NKCC), which is also the target
of loop diuretics. The negatively charged interstitium attracts positive cations like Caþþ, Mgþþ and Naþ, which are also reabsorbed
via a paracellular way. Also in the loop of Henle, the paracellular pathway is responsible for a relevant proportion (50%) of the Naþ
reabsorption. ADH, PTH, calcitonin, glucagon and adrenaline increase the Naþ and Clþ reabsorption in the TAL. On the contrary,
